# PicoCalc LCD Readback

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A small mini-project for the ClockworkPi PicoCalc: can you read pixel
data back **off** the LCD, not just write to it?

`picocalc-text-starter` (by Blair Leduc) only ever writes to the ST7365P
controller's frame memory (`lcd_blit()`). This project adds the missing
other half, `lcd_unblit()`, a small console test tool to prove it
actually reads back what was written, and — built on top of that — a
screenshot-to-SD-card feature: save a rectangle, or the whole screen, as
a BMP file, and load one back.

## What's here

- **`lcd_readback.c`/`.h`** — `lcd_unblit()`, the read-side mirror of
  `lcd_blit()`. Built entirely on `lcd.h`'s existing public pins, command
  macros, and `lcd_write_cmd()`/`lcd_write_data()`, plus `hardware/spi.h`
  directly for the one thing the vendored driver doesn't expose: driving a
  read cycle (RAMRD, `0x2E`). The vendored `picocalc-text-starter-main/`
  tree itself is untouched.
- **`bmp.c`/`.h`** — screenshots to SD card: `bmp_save_screenshot()`/
  `picocalc_screenshot()` (the whole screen) write an uncompressed 24-bit
  BMP; `bmp_load_and_blit()` reads one back and displays it. Both read
  and write **one LCD row at a time** — never a whole-screen pixel buffer
  in RAM (320x320 pixels would be 200KB, more than half the RP2040's
  total SRAM). Built on `fat32_*()` (`fat32.h`, also by Blair Leduc).
- **`main.c`** — a console REPL (same shape as the starter's own
  `main.c`, via `picocalc_init()`): write a rectangle of pixels, read it
  back, compare; save/load screenshots. See `help` at the prompt.
- **`readback_config.h`** — the tunable constants, with the reasoning
  behind each one (datasheet, or hardware-confirmed — see below).

## Commands

```
test [w h count]        write random pixels, read them back, compare
pattern                  draw a visible checkerboard, verify it, leave it
                         on screen for a photo
raw x y w h              read back a rectangle and dump it as hex (no write)
solid x y w h rrggbb     fill a rectangle with one exact RGB565 colour
rawbytes x y w h n       dump n raw RAMRD bytes, no interpretation;
                         for figuring out an on-wire byte layout by hand
screenshot x y w h       save a rectangle to SD as SCRNxxxx.BMP
loadbmp file x y         load a BMP from SD and display it at (x,y)
screentest x y w h destx desty
                         round trip: screenshot to SD, close it, reopen
                         it, display it elsewhere; proves the whole
                         save/load path works, not just lcd_unblit()
fullscreenshot           picocalc_screenshot(): the whole screen to SD
sdstatus                 SD card presence, mount status, free space
bootsel                  reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode
exit (or quit)           leave for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu (asks the loader for its
                         menu through the watchdog scratch registers; with no loader
                         installed the program just restarts)
help                     list commands
```

`test` with no arguments runs one pass over a 64x64 test rectangle. The
test rectangle always sits well below the console's own text rows, so
printed output and the pixel test never overlap on screen.

## How the readback actually works

Confirmed on real RP2040 hardware (2026-09-28), via `solid` + `rawbytes`:
fill a rectangle with one exact colour, then dump the raw bytes RAMRD
(`0x2E`) sends back with no interpretation and read the repeating pattern
off by eye.

With `COLMOD` set to 16-bit/pixel (`0x55`, what `lcd_init()` always uses),
`RAMRD` reads pixels back in that **same 16-bit RGB565 format**
`lcd_blit()` writes them in — two bytes per pixel, big-endian,
byte-for-byte identical to what was written. `lcd_unblit()` just
reassembles the two bytes; no bit-shifting or channel-width reconstruction
needed. (An earlier version of this file said frame memory was natively
18 bits/pixel and reads came back as three bytes per pixel, one per
colour component — that was a wrong reading of the ST7365P datasheet,
which describes the read byte format ambiguously enough to get this
wrong on paper; a hardware test rectangle failed on every single pixel
under that version, which is what prompted actually looking at the raw
bytes instead of the datasheet.)

One thing the write path doesn't need to care about, also confirmed the
same way: the very first byte clocked out after the `RAMRD` command
really is a **dummy byte** with no pixel data in it, and must be
discarded before the real, repeating pixel data starts.

Reads still run **much slower** than writes: `lcd_blit()` drives the bus
at `LCD_BAUDRATE` (75MHz); `lcd_unblit()` drops to `LCD_READ_BAUDRATE`
(`readback_config.h`, 1MHz) for the read and restores the normal speed
afterward. 1MHz is now confirmed to work, but **not** confirmed to be
necessary — nobody's tried raising it yet.

## Screenshots (`bmp.c`)

`screenshot`/`fullscreenshot` read a rectangle (or the whole screen) with
`lcd_unblit()` and write it as a plain, uncompressed 24-bit BMP
(`BITMAPFILEHEADER`+`BITMAPINFOHEADER`, `BI_RGB`, bottom-up row order —
the most widely compatible BMP shape) to a new file on the SD card, named
`SCRNxxxx.BMP` with `xxxx` a random 4-digit uppercase hex number (a fresh
number is tried if that exact name is already taken). `loadbmp` reads one
back with `fat32_*()` and `lcd_blit()`s it onto the screen.

Both directions work **one LCD row at a time**, never a whole-image pixel
buffer: a full 320x320 screenshot would need 200KB held in RAM at once if
it didn't, more than half the RP2040's total SRAM. Each row is converted
between the LCD's 16-bit RGB565 and the BMP's 24-bit BGR (bit-replicating
each 5- or 6-bit channel up to 8 bits) and written or read immediately,
so memory use stays a small, fixed handful of bytes regardless of image
size.

## Building

Firmware only (RP2040/RP2350) — this project is inherently about one
specific LCD controller's low-level SPI protocol, so there's no
meaningful "hardware-independent" version of `lcd_unblit()` itself to
write; `main.c`'s own test/compare logic has no display-specific code in
it, so that half stays as portable as the rest of this codebase.

From a terminal with `PICO_SDK_PATH` set:

    cmake -B build -G Ninja
    ninja -C build

Output: `lcd-readback-RP2040.uf2` / `-RP2350.uf2`, copied to the
top-level project folder. Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2` BOOTSEL
drive.

## Status

Working on real RP2040 hardware as of 2026-09-28, including a
screenshot/reload round trip (`screentest`) and a full 320x320
`fullscreenshot`. `LCD_READ_BAUDRATE` is the one remaining unconfirmed
number — see `CLAUDE.md`, which also has the full story of two real bugs
(one in `fat32.c`, one in this project's own `lcd_readback.c`) found
getting `fullscreenshot` working.
